en: Tell me, best of the twice-born, the rites of refinement beginning with the birth rite for each class in order, and the duties of the stages of life.
Conception, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, the birth rite, first feeding of grain, tonsure and the tying of the munja-grass girdle:
the fault of the seed and of the womb is wiped away from the twice-born by study, vows, fire offerings, knowledge of the three Vedas, sacrifice and hearing.
By the great sacrifices and by sacrifices, the body is made fit for Brahman. Listen with one mind, O king, to how that body is made so.
The birth rite of a male is ordained before the cutting of the navel cord, and with mantras he is given a taste of gold, honey and ghee.
Some, O king, want the naming on the tenth day, others on the twelfth, others when the month is complete,
and other wise men say on the eighteenth day, on a holy day, at a good hour, under a star with good qualities.
For a Brahmin, my dear, the name should be auspicious, like Shivasharma; for a Kshatriya it should be distinguished, like Indurvarma.
For a Vaishya it should suggest wealth, and for a Shudra it should be lowly: Dhanavardhana for a Vaishya, Sarvadasa for the low-born.

first: मनुना च तथा प्रोक्तं नाम्नो लक्षणमुत्तमम् ।
en: Manu has also given the best mark of a name: for a Brahmin it should have "sharma", for a king it should carry the sense of protection,
for a Vaishya the sense of prosperity, for a Shudra the sense of service. For women it should be easy to say, not harsh, clear in meaning and pleasing,
auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and carrying a blessing. On the twelfth day, O best of kings, the child is taken out of the house.

first: चतुर्थे मासि कर्त्तव्यं तथान्येषां मतं विभो ।
en: It should be done in the fourth month, others hold, O lord. The first feeding of grain is in the sixth month, or as the family finds auspicious.
The tonsure of all the twice-born should be done in order, in the first or third year, O joy of the Kurus.
One should perform the initiation of a Brahmin in the eighth year from conception; that of a Kshatriya, O king, should be set in the eleventh year from conception.
The vow for a Vaishya is set in the twelfth year from conception. For a Brahmin who desires spiritual glory it may be done in the fifth,

first: बलार्थिना तथा राज्ञः षष्ठे ऽब्दे कार्यमेव हि ।
en: and for a king who desires strength in the sixth, and for a Vaishya who desires wealth in the eighth, O joy of the Kurus.
For a Brahmin the Savitri [initiation] does not pass until sixteen; for a Kshatriya until twenty-two; for a Vaishya until twenty-four.
Those who go beyond that time without the rite, O king, are fallen from the Savitri and are called Vratyas, except through the Vratya-stoma sacrifice.
With such impure persons, even in distress, one should never form a Vedic or marriage tie together with Brahmins.
Students' skins, O king, are of three kinds: the black antelope, the ruru deer and the goat, for Brahmin, Kshatriya and Vaishya respectively.
They should wear various garments in order: for Brahmin, Kshatriya and Vaishya, those of hemp, linen and the like.

first: मौञ्जी त्रिवृत्समा श्लक्ष्णा कार्या विप्रस्य मेखला ।
en: The Brahmin's girdle should be of munja grass, three-stranded, smooth; the Kshatriya's of a bowstring fibre, and the Vaishya's of hemp thread.
If munja is not found, it should be made of kusha, ashmantaka or balvaja grass, tied with one, three or five knots.
The sacred thread of a Brahmin should be of cotton, three-stranded and twisted upward; the king's of hemp thread; the Vaishya's of sheep's wool.

first: पुष्कराणि तथा चैषां भवन्ति त्रिविधानि तु ।
en: Their staffs are likewise of three kinds: for the Brahmin of bilva and palasha wood, and a third of plaksha, O king;
for the Kshatriya of vata and khadira, and another of vetasa; for the Vaishya of pilu and udumbara, and also of ashvattha.
These staffs, O mighty-armed one, they may rightly carry. A Brahmin's staff should be made to reach the hair, by measure;
the king's should reach the forehead, the Vaishya's the nose. All should be straight, pleasant to look at, bark intact,
not frightening to people, and not spoiled by fire. Taking the staff he likes and standing before the sun,
and honouring his teacher properly, the initiated best of the twice-born should go begging as the rule says. The Brahmin should put "bhavat" first [when begging],
the Kshatriya in the middle, the Vaishya at the end. He should beg first from his mother, sister or mother's sister,

first: भिक्षेत भैक्ष्यं प्रथमं या चैनं नावमानयेत् ।
en: who will not scorn him, and she should put gold, silver or food in his bowl.
Having then gathered alms as needed, without deceit, he should offer it to the teacher, rinse his mouth, and eat facing east, pure.
Facing east one eats long life; facing south, fame; facing west, prosperity; facing north, truth.
The twice-born, O king, should rinse his mouth and eat his food with a calm mind, and after eating rinse again properly and touch the openings of the head with water.
One should always honour the food and eat it without blaming it. Seeing it, one should be glad and pleased, O descendant of Bharata.
One should greet it and then eat, so Manu said. Food honoured always gives strength and vigour.
Food eaten without honour destroys both. One should not give leftovers to anyone, nor eat between meals.
One who, out of greed, eats in between meals, O best of kings, is ruined here and in the next world, as the Vaishya named Dhanavardhana was long ago.
How did he, best of the twice-born, break his meal earlier? What is the break in food, and how was it done?
Long ago in the Krita age, O king, a Vaishya lived at Pushkara, named Dhanavardhana, rich in wealth and grain.
In the hot season, O best of kings, after the offering to all gods, together with his sons, brothers, friends and relatives, he took a meal of food to be chewed and eaten.
Then, as he ate, there was a great sound, a piteous one, O tiger of the Kurus, and he ran toward it.
Leaving his meal, he went outside the house. The sound then vanished, and he came back into the house.
Taking the same dish, O king, he ate the rest of the food that remained.

first: भुक्त्वा स शतधा जातस्तस्मिन्नेव क्षणे नृप ।
en: Having eaten it, he fell into a hundred pieces at that very moment, O king. Therefore one should never eat food in between.
One should not overeat, and should never go about with leftover food on him. Overeating makes a [bad] juice, and from that juice disease arises.
Bathing, giving, prayer, fire offerings and worship of ancestors and gods do not happen for people when the juice has formed, O best of the Bharatas.
Overeating gives ill health, shortens life, bars heaven, is unholy and disliked by the world. Therefore one should avoid it.
A Brahmin who has leftover food on him becomes accessible to Yakshas, spirits, Pishachas and Rakshasas, O best of kings, without doubt.
Therefore one should take refuge in purity; through purity one is glad and lives happily here. So says the Vedic scripture. (text unclear)
How does a Brahmin become pure, and how impure? Tell me this, best of Brahmins; my curiosity is great.
A Brahmin becomes pure by rinsing his mouth, O best of the Bharatas, properly, as the rule says, O tiger of the Kurus. So he should follow the rule.
Tell me fully, Brahmin, the rule of rinsing, by which a twice-born Brahmin, having sipped water, gains purity.

first: साधु पृष्टोऽस्मि राजेन्द्र शृणु विप्रो यथा भवेत् ।
en: You have asked well, O best of kings. Hear how a Brahmin becomes pure, O tiger of the Bharatas, by what rule.

first: प्रक्षाल्य हस्तौ पादौ च प्राङ्मुखोदङ्मुखोऽपि वा ।
en: Having washed hands and feet, he should sit in a clean place facing east or north, with the right arm drawn in,
between the knees, O mighty-armed one, wearing the sacred thread, feet level, hair tied up,
not standing, not talking, not looking around, not hurrying or angry, O king, setting such things far aside.
By rinsing with clear water he becomes pure: not hot, not foamy, nor water mixed with dirt,
nor water lacking colour, taste and smell, nor with bubbles; a wise man should not rinse with such, O king.
Five sacred spots are told in a Brahmin's right hand: the divine spot, the ancestors' spot, the Brahma spot, O giver of honour,
the Prajapati spot, and another called the Saumya spot. The line above the base of the thumb, O lord of the earth,
is called the Brahma spot by Vasishtha and other best of the twice-born. The Kaya spot is at the base of the little finger, the divine spot at the fingertips,
the ancestors' spot between the forefinger and thumb, and the Saumya spot in the middle of the palm, praised for rites for gods.
Worship of gods, the food offering and the casting [of offerings] one should do with the divine spot, O lift of the Kuru line.
The pouring out of grain, O king, and also the purifying [rite], and the offering of parched grain, one should do with the Prajapati spot.
Touching the water jar and eating curds, a wise man should always do with the Saumya spot, O best of kings.
Offering to the ancestors should be done by the wise with the ancestors' spot, and touching [the body] with the Brahma spot is best.
Making the fingers close together, one-pointed and with a good mind, the twice-born who sips water three times without any sound from the mouth,

first: शृणु यत्फलमाप्नोति प्रीणाति च यथा सुरान् ।
en: hear what reward he gains and how he pleases the gods. By the first sip, the Rigveda is satisfied;
by the second, he pleases the Yajurveda, O descendant of Bharata; by the third, he pleases the Samaveda.
When he first wipes the mouth, from the base of the right thumb, the Atharvaveda is pleased, O king, without doubt.
When he wipes it a second time, the histories and Puranas are pleased; when the twice-born sprinkles the head, O best of kings,

first: तेन प्रीणाति वै रुद्रं शिखामालभ्य वै ऋषीन् ।
en: he pleases Rudra; touching the crown he pleases the sages; when he touches the eyes, the sun is pleased.
By touching the nose he pleases the wind, without doubt. When a Brahmin touches the ear, he pleases the directions.

first: यमं कुबेरं वरुणं वासवं चाग्निमेव च ।
en: By touching the arm he pleases Yama, Kubera, Varuna, Indra and Agni.
By touching the navel, the knot of the life breaths, he pleases them, O best of kings. So says the Vedic scripture.

first: अभिषिञ्चति यत्पादौ विष्णुं प्रीणाति तेन वै ।
en: By sprinkling the feet he pleases Vishnu. When he lets the water fall on the ground, O giver of honour,
he pleases Vasuki and the other Nagas, O descendant of Bharata. The drops that fall on the earth here, O ruler of men,
please the four kinds of beings. With the thumb and forefinger he should touch the eyes, O king;
with the ring finger and thumb the nose; with the middle finger and thumb he should touch the mouth, O best of the Bharatas;
with the little finger and thumb he touches the ear, O king; with the fingers the arm, and with the thumb the [auspicious spot].
The navel, O best of the Kuru line, and the head with all the fingers.

first: अनामिका तथा सूर्यः कनिष्ठा माघवा विभो ।
en: The ring finger is the sun, the little finger is Indra, O lord; the middle finger should be known as Prajapati, therefore, O best of the Bharatas.
A Brahmin who rinses in this way ever pleases the world, and all the gods and the worlds too, without doubt, my dear.

first: तस्मात्पूज्यः सदा विप्रः सर्वदेवमयो हि सः ।
en: Therefore a Brahmin is always to be honoured, for he is made of all the gods. He should always rinse with the Brahma spot, the Brahmin's holy place,
or with the Kaya or Traidashika spot, but never with the ancestors' spot. A Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart, a king by water reaching the throat,
a Vaishya by water that is drunk, a Shudra by water that touches only the lips. When the right hand is raised, the wise call him "upavitin" [with the thread over the left shoulder],
with the left, "pracinavitin"; and with the thread at the neck, "nivitin". The girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread and water jar,
if lost or spoiled, one who knows the mantras should discard and take new ones. Wearing the thread properly, he should always rinse, within the knees, O lord of the earth.

first: एवं तु विप्रो ह्याचान्तः शुचितां याति भारत ।
en: In this way a Brahmin, having rinsed, gains purity, O descendant of Bharata. And these lines in the middle of a Brahmin's palm, O descendant of Bharata,
should be known as all the rivers beginning with the Ganga, O best of the Bharatas. The joints of the fingers, know, are the mountains.
The right hand of a Brahmin is made of all the gods, O king. The rule for touching water with the hand has been told to you, O lord of the earth.

first: एषु सर्वेषु लोकेषु येनाचान्तो दिवं व्रजेत् ॥ ९५ ॥
en: In all these worlds, by whom one has rinsed, one may go to heaven.
